metadata.title: ECIS — Episode 16: How Far Ahead Can You See?

beats.narration_text: Fifteen episodes of asking what an earnings call is telling you right now. This one asks a harder question — not what the signal is, but how far ahead of it you can see. I'm Anjana.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself

props.command: ECIS can tell me a company is likely to revise its guidance. It cannot tell me when, it only ever looks one quarter out, and it has no idea what the call was actually about. Can it forecast at several horizons at once, predict the timing rather than just the event, and track what management chooses to talk about?
output: one horizon becomes four, and the bands widen honestly
whether a revision comes becomes when it comes
and the answer arrives with its working shown

beats.narration_text: ECIS extracts guidance signals from earnings calls using four readers weighted by a five-dimension triangulator. Tree-based ensembles, LSTM, and GRU models predict guidance revisions, with a Hidden Markov Model providing market regime context. Uncertainty quantification and selective abstention keep low-confidence forecasts out of the output. Analyst intelligence normalizes dodge scores by question difficulty. Cross-company contagion tracks language shifts propagating across sectors. And a RAG-augmented agent answers natural language queries by citing both transcripts and structured data. This week, the system looks further ahead — and starts asking not just whether, but when.

props.sparkLine: This week: it looks further ahead.

beats.narration_text: Until now, every forecast looked one quarter ahead. A Temporal Fusion Transformer changes that. It produces probabilistic fan charts at one, two, five, and ten quarter horizons — wider bands further out, tighter bands close in. Attention mechanisms let it look back selectively, learning which historical quarters matter most for each prediction. And Prophet decomposes each signal into trend, seasonality, and residual — isolating the long-term direction from repeating cycles and random noise. Some companies hedge more before every fiscal year-end. That's seasonality, not deterioration. Now the system knows the difference.

Predicting that a company will revise guidance is useful. Predicting when is better. Time-to-revision modeling treats each company as a countdown — ticking forward in quarters until the event happens. A statistical model estimates risk factors for each feature: how much does rising hedging momentum or increasing dodge scores accelerate that countdown? Per-company timing curves show the probability of guidance remaining unchanged over time. When the curve drops steeply, the company enters a high-alert window — revision likely within one to two quarters.

Earnings calls aren't just about how management speaks — they're about what management speaks about. BERTopic extracts themes from the full transcript corpus per sector per quarter. It tracks when new topics emerge, when established ones fade, and when a company's topic mix diverges from its peers. If an entire sector is discussing cost optimization and one company is still focused on expansion, that divergence is a signal. Topic shift detection measures quarter-over-quarter changes and flags anomalies — sudden pivots in what management chooses to talk about.

props.sparkLine: Not how they said it — what about.

beats.narration_text: The agent can now think in steps. A complex question like "compare hedging trends across the sector, then explain the outlier" becomes a chain: retrieve the data, run the comparison, identify the outlier, pull the transcript context, and synthesize an explanation. Each step's output feeds the next. The final response includes a comparison table with source citations — every claim linked back to the data point that supports it. The system doesn't just answer. It shows its work.

Twenty-one phases in, the system's field of vision keeps expanding. Multi-horizon forecasting sees one to ten quarters ahead. Time-to-revision modeling predicts when revisions will happen, not just whether. Topic modeling tracks what management chooses to discuss — and flags when that changes abruptly. And the agent reasons through complex queries step by step, citing its sources along the way. The question isn't just what's the signal. It's how far ahead can you see? Next week, we keep building.

props.sparkLine: How far ahead can you see?

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Every forecast this system made until now answered one question at one distance — what happens next quarter. A temporal fusion transformer turns that into four answers at four distances, each carrying a band that widens honestly the further out it looks. Prophet does the unglamorous half: it separates the companies that hedge before every year-end, which is the difference between a signal and a calendar. Time-to-revision replaces whether with when, and when is the version a desk can actually act on. Topic modelling finally reads what the call was about rather than only how it was said. And the agent shows its working — five steps, each one cited back to the data that supports it.

show.event: 0.5s lead pause, then ClaudeVerdictArtifact card builds in

lines: a forecast stops being one number at one distance
a year-end bump is no longer read as decay
whether a revision comes is replaced by when
what the call was about is finally a feature
and the answer arrives with its steps and its sources

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Nearly every model you have produces one answer at one distance. Paste this into Claude and work through three things — whether you should be forecasting at several horizons instead of one, whether your real question is when rather than whether, and what you are ignoring about what your data is actually about.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Your turn.'; prompt types itself

props.command: I produce a prediction that answers one question at one point in time. Can you help me: one, work out whether I should be forecasting at several horizons instead of one, and what my uncertainty bands would have to do as the horizon grows for them to be honest rather than decorative; two, tell me whether the useful question is actually WHEN my event happens rather than WHETHER, and what a time-to-event model would need from the data I already have; and three, check whether I am only modelling HOW things are said or measured while ignoring WHAT they are about — because that is usually the feature sitting in plain sight.
